title: Ezekiel 41:15–26
context: The guide finishes measuring the house and its surroundings and the prophet describes its interior. The walls are paneled with wood and carved throughout with cherubim and palm trees, each cherub having two faces, a man's face toward one palm and a young lion's face toward the other. The nave's doorposts are square, and before the inner room stands a wooden altar, which the guide calls “the table that is before the LORD.” The nave and the sanctuary each have double doors carved like the walls. The chapter closes with the windows and palm trees on the sides of the porch. Solomon's temple was also carved with “cherubim, palm trees, and open flowers” (1 Kings 6:29). Readers who take the vision in the ways named at 40:1–16 all find meaning in these details, and both traditions include each view.

verses.text: He measured the length of the building before the separate place which was at its back, and its galleries on the one side and on the other side, one hundred cubits from the inner temple, and the porches of the court,
verses.arminianNotes: “He measured the length of the building before the separate place which was at its back.” Arminian readers see the guide confirming the building's length as one hundred cubits, with its galleries on each side.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers note that this repeats the measures of verses 12–13. The repetition rounds off the measurements before the description of the interior begins.

verses.text: the thresholds, and the closed windows, and the galleries around on their three stories, opposite the threshold, with wood ceilings all around, and from the ground up to the windows, (now the windows were covered),
verses.arminianNotes: “the thresholds, and the closed windows, and the galleries around on their three stories.” Arminian readers see the inside of the house paneled “with wood ceilings all around,” from the ground up to the windows.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers note that the house is fully finished inside. The richness of the interior suggests honor and beauty fitting for the place of God's presence.

verses.text: to the space above the door, even to the inner house, and outside, and by all the wall all around inside and outside, by measure.
verses.arminianNotes: “to the space above the door, even to the inner house.” Arminian readers see the walls finished inside and out, “by measure,” throughout the house.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers note that the phrase “by measure” stresses that nothing was arbitrary. The vision's careful measuring continues even into the decoration.

verses.text: It was made with cherubim and palm trees. A palm tree was between cherub and cherub, and every cherub had two faces,
verses.arminianNotes: “It was made with cherubim and palm trees.” Arminian readers see carved cherubim alternating with palm trees, “every cherub had two faces.”
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers note that cherubim guarded the way to the tree of life in Genesis, and many see a garden picture here. Solomon's temple also had carved cherubim and palm trees (1 Kings 6:29).

verses.text: so that there was the face of a man toward the palm tree on the one side, and the face of a young lion toward the palm tree on the other side. It was made like this through all the house all around.
verses.arminianNotes: “so that there was the face of a man toward the palm tree on the one side.” Arminian readers see each cherub with a man's face and “the face of a young lion,” turned toward palm trees on either side.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers note that the cherubim in Ezekiel 1:10 had four faces, including a man and a lion. Here the carved figures show two. The text does not explain the difference.

verses.text: Cherubim and palm trees were made from the ground to above the door. The wall of the temple was like this.
verses.arminianNotes: “Cherubim and palm trees were made from the ground to above the door.” Arminian readers see the decoration covering the walls of the temple from floor to above the doorway.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers note the phrase “The wall of the temple was like this.” The whole sanctuary is marked with signs that many readers connect with God's presence and life.

verses.text: The door posts of the nave were squared. As for the face of the nave, its appearance was as the appearance of the temple.
verses.arminianNotes: “The door posts of the nave were squared.” Arminian readers see the doorposts of the main hall shaped square, with the nave's appearance matching the rest of the temple.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers note that the square shape recurs throughout the vision, from courts to doorposts. The consistent forms convey order and completeness.

verses.text: The altar was of wood, three cubits high, and its length two cubits. Its corners, its base, and its walls were of wood. He said to me, “This is the table that is before the LORD.”
verses.arminianNotes: He said to me, “This is the table that is before the LORD.” Arminian readers see a wooden altar, “three cubits high,” called a table set in the LORD's presence.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers note that readers differ on whether this is the table for the bread of the presence (Exodus 25:30) or an altar of incense. The guide calls it “the table that is before the LORD,” and leaves it there.

verses.text: The temple and the sanctuary had two doors.
verses.arminianNotes: “The temple and the sanctuary had two doors.” Arminian readers see doors for both the main hall and the inner room, marking separate stages of approach.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers note that the doors distinguish the nave from the most holy place. Hebrews 9:24 speaks of holy places “made with hands” as “representations of the true,” which some readers apply here.

verses.text: The doors had two leaves each, two turning leaves: two for the one door, and two leaves for the other.
verses.arminianNotes: “The doors had two leaves each, two turning leaves.” Arminian readers see folding double doors at each entrance, with two leaves on each door.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers note that the doors could fold open. The detail shows a real, functioning structure in the prophet's vision, whatever its final meaning.

verses.text: There were made on them, on the doors of the nave, cherubim and palm trees, like those made on the walls. There was a threshold of wood on the face of the porch outside.
verses.arminianNotes: “There were made on them, on the doors of the nave, cherubim and palm trees.” Arminian readers see the doors carved like the walls, and a wooden threshold “on the face of the porch outside.”
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers note that the decoration is consistent from walls to doors. The same signs of life and holiness mark every surface of the sanctuary.

verses.text: There were closed windows and palm trees on the one side and on the other side, on the sides of the porch. This is how the side rooms of the temple and the thresholds were arranged.
verses.arminianNotes: “There were closed windows and palm trees on the one side and on the other side.” Arminian readers see the porch finished with windows and palm trees, closing the description of the house.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers note the closing summary: “This is how the side rooms of the temple and the thresholds were arranged.” The account of the house is complete, preparing for the rooms of chapter 42 and the glory's return in chapter 43.
